namesOverTime.name: Ichirouganaim

from.note: Date is a rough marker for the pre-contact centuries, not an event.

namesOverTime.note: The name is recorded only in later tradition and its meaning is disputed; no Indigenous written record survives.

namesOverTime.name: Los Barbados

from.note: Usually credited to the Portuguese navigator Pedro a Campos; the exact voyage and year are uncertain.

namesOverTime.note: 'The bearded ones', from the island's bearded fig trees.

modernSuccessors.name: Barbados
modernSuccessors.note: A parliamentary republic since 30 November 2021; still a Commonwealth member.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: Barbados is one island with no land neighbours: its extent never changed in 339 years of British rule.

acquisitions.how: The ship William and John landed about 80 English settlers and ten Africans it had seized at sea on an uninhabited coast, at the place they named Jamestown, now Holetown.

counterparties.name: Kalinago and Arawak peoples
counterparties.lost: They lost the island itself: Spanish and Portuguese slave raiding had emptied Barbados during the 1500s, so the English found land already cleared of its owners.
counterparties.note: Archaeology shows Amerindian settlement for well over a thousand years before 1500. 'Uninhabited in 1627' is true; 'never inhabited' is false, and the difference matters.

instrument.name: Letters patent to James Hay, Earl of Carlisle, over the Caribbee Islands
instrument.note: The grant was made after the settlers had already landed, and was disputed for years by a rival grantee, the Earl of Pembroke.

people.name: Henry Powell
people.role: captain of the William and John; led the first settlement party

people.name: James Hay, Earl of Carlisle
people.role: proprietor who held the island as a private grant from Charles I

acquisitions.resistance: There was no resident population to resist in 1627; the violence that emptied the island had been done by Spanish slave raiders a century earlier.

contested.note: An earlier English ship under John Powell claimed the island in 1625; some accounts date the colony from then. Historians date the colony from the 1627 landing because that is when people stayed.

evidence.author: Richard S. Dunn
evidence.work: Sugar and Slaves: The Rise of the Planter Class in the English West Indies, 1624-1713
evidence.supports: Date, personnel and proprietary basis of the 1627 settlement.

statusPeriods.label: Private colony of the Earl of Carlisle
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The island belonged to a court favourite who appointed the governor and took rent from every settler; the Crown ruled Barbados only at one remove.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bridgetown, under a proprietor in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Only Protestant male freeholders with ten acres or more could vote; the House of Assembly first met in 1639.
statusPeriods.note: In 1651-52 the planters sided with the exiled Stuarts and were blockaded into submission by Sir George Ayscue's fleet; the Charter of Barbados, signed at Oistins in January 1652, confirmed the Assembly's right to tax.

statusPeriods.label: Royal colony with a planter Assembly
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown bought out the proprietor and appointed the governor, but an elected planter Assembly voted the taxes, so London governed by bargaining with the men who owned the plantations and the people on them.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bridgetown, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: A property franchise excluded almost everyone: enslaved people entirely until 1834, and most Barbadians afterwards. Universal adult suffrage came only in 1951.
statusPeriods.note: From 1833 to 1885 the governor at Bridgetown was also governor-in-chief of the Windward Islands, which is why Barbados appears on old maps as a regional capital. Barbados joined the West Indies Federation in 1958 and left when it collapsed in 1962.

statusPeriods.label: Full internal self-government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Barbadians ran their own government under a Premier, Errol Barrow, while Britain kept only defence and foreign affairs for five more years.

departures.how: After a constitutional conference in London in June 1966, Britain legislated Barbados into independence and the flag changed at midnight in Bridgetown with nobody killed.

led.name: Errol Barrow
led.role: Premier, then first Prime Minister; led the independence negotiations

led.name: Grantley Adams
led.role: opposition leader who argued independence should come through a federation, not alone

cost.note: No one died. Barbados is the counter-example students need: decolonisation was not always violent, and the absence of violence here has its own causes worth explaining.

departures.borders: The borders did nothing. An island colony with no land neighbours became a state with exactly the coastline it had in 1627.

instrument.name: Barbados Independence Act 1966
instrument.note: Royal assent 17 November 1966; independence took effect on 30 November 1966.

evidence.author: Hilary McD. Beckles
evidence.work: A History of Barbados: From Amerindian Settlement to Caribbean Single Market
evidence.supports: Course of the independence negotiations and the 1966 settlement.

slavery.note: Sugar made Barbados the richest English colony and enslaved Africans made the sugar: by 1680 they were the majority of the population, and they stayed the majority ever after.

abolitionDate.note: The Slave Trade Act 1807 ended British trafficking; it did not free anyone already enslaved.

emancipationDate.note: The Slavery Abolition Act took effect on 1 August 1834, but imposed four more years of unpaid 'apprenticeship'. Full freedom came on 1 August 1838.

toll.money: About £1.7 million was paid in 1837 to Barbadian slave-owners as compensation for losing their property in people. The people themselves received nothing.
toll.note: Totals of Africans landed in Barbados vary because the island was also a re-export market that sold captives on to other colonies; the range follows the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database. About 83,000 people were freed in Barbados in 1834.

populationTransfer.note: Two forced migrations built the colony: hundreds of thousands of Africans trafficked across the Atlantic, and thousands of Irish and Scottish prisoners shipped out under Cromwell in the 1650s.

violence.note: Bussa's rebellion in April 1816 was put down in four days; several hundred enslaved people were killed in the fighting, executed after it, or transported off the island.

commonwealth.note: Barbados removed the British monarch as head of state on 30 November 2021, exactly 55 years after independence, and stayed in the Commonwealth.

consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar dominated the economy for three centuries and then collapsed; tourism and offshore finance replaced it within one generation.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, an Assembly meeting continuously since 1639, and Anglican parish boundaries still divide the island.

peak.populationNote: 1960 census, the last full count before independence. In 1680 the population was about 70,000, of whom roughly two thirds were enslaved.

evidence.author: Hilary McD. Beckles
evidence.work: A History of Barbados: From Amerindian Settlement to Caribbean Single Market
evidence.supports: Overall narrative from Amerindian settlement to independence.

evidence.author: Richard S. Dunn
evidence.work: Sugar and Slaves: The Rise of the Planter Class in the English West Indies, 1624-1713
evidence.supports: The sugar revolution, planter society and the 1661 slave code.

evidence.author: Hilary McD. Beckles
evidence.publisher: University of the West Indies, Department of History

contested.note: Historians disagree about how completely Barbados was emptied of Amerindian people before 1627, and about how many Africans were landed there as against re-exported. Both uncertainties are shown in this record rather than smoothed away.

pedagogy.hook: By 1660 this 430-square-kilometre island was worth more to England than all of its North American colonies put together.

misconception.belief: Irish people shipped to Barbados in the 1650s were 'Irish slaves', the same as enslaved Africans.
misconception.correction: Thousands of Irish and Scottish prisoners were transported to Barbados and worked brutally, but as indentured servants for a fixed term. The 1661 Barbados slave code made African enslavement lifelong, inheritable and enforceable by mutilation, and gave the enslaved no legal personhood at all. The conditions overlapped; the legal categories did not.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Barbados invented the model the rest of the British Caribbean copied: monoculture sugar, mass enslavement, and a written slave code that Jamaica in 1664 and South Carolina in 1691 adapted almost word for word.

keyDates.what: The Barbados slave code, copied across the empire
Full emancipation, after four years of 'apprenticeship'

events.title: Bussa's Rebellion
events.summary: On Easter Sunday 1816 enslaved people across southern and eastern Barbados rose, burning cane fields on more than seventy estates. Martial law and the West India Regiment crushed the rising in four days.
events.significance: It was the first of three great British Caribbean risings (Barbados 1816, Demerara 1823, Jamaica 1831-32) that convinced Parliament slavery could not be held down indefinitely, and it hardened the abolitionist case in London.

places.name: Bridgetown
places.note: Seat of the governor who declared martial law.

people.name: Bussa
people.role: African-born ranger at Bayley's plantation; led the rising and was killed in the fighting

people.name: Nanny Grigg
people.role: enslaved woman at Simmons plantation who, witnesses said, told others freedom had already been granted and would have to be taken

people.name: Washington Franklin
people.role: free man of colour tried and executed as an organiser

people.name: James Leith
people.role: governor who declared martial law and directed the suppression

toll.note: About fifty enslaved people died fighting, roughly seventy were executed in the field and some three hundred after trial; 170 more were transported off the island. Two people died on the militia's side. Totals differ between accounts.

pedagogy.hook: The rebels believed emancipation had already been granted in London and was being hidden from them by the planters.

misconception.belief: Enslaved people were freed by Parliament and abolitionists acting on their behalf.
misconception.correction: Freedom was fought for from below as well as argued for in London. Barbados 1816, Demerara 1823 and Jamaica 1831-32 each raised the cost of holding slavery in place, and the Abolition Act followed the Jamaican rising by eighteen months.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows resistance as a cause of abolition, not just a footnote to it.

evidence.author: Hilary McD. Beckles
evidence.publisher: University of the West Indies, Department of History
evidence.supports: Course of the rising, its leaders and its suppression.

contested.note: The death toll and Bussa's own role come mostly from the planters' own inquiry of 1818, a hostile source; the number executed after trial is especially uncertain.
